A second instrument takes lesson 81’s 1.04 independent bets to 1.28 at the correlation equities actually run at. Turning one leg short takes the same pair’s standard deviation from 0.9810 to 0.1940.

Lesson 81 left the course’s own book carrying 1.04 independent bets on one instrument, and the obvious repair is a second instrument. Run lesson 71’s divisor on it and the repair is smaller than it looks: two rules on each of two instruments is four positions, and at a cross-correlation of zero that is 2.08 bets rather than four. Nothing correlates at zero, and one row down from the middle, at 0.6, it is 1.28. Then turn one leg over, which is the thing this course has never allowed a rule to do. Two equal positions at a correlation of 0.9247 have a standard deviation of 0.9810 when both are long and 0.1940 when one is short, a factor of 5.06. The 0.9247 that collapsed the book is the same number that makes the spread worth holding, and lesson 74 measured it on this course’s own rules.
, for the 0.9247 and for how far it moves,
, for the 1.04 the repair is meant to fix.

Lesson 71’s divisor takes a count of positions and an average correlation between them and returns the number of independent bets they amount to: the count divided by one plus the count less one times the average. Two positions at 0.9247 give 1.0391, which is the 1.04 lesson 75 licensed and lesson 81 graded. The formula does not care what the positions are. It cares only how alike they move.

So put the same two rules on a second instrument and run it again. Four positions, six pairs. Two of those pairs are within an instrument and carry lesson 74’s 0.9247. The other four cross between instruments and carry whatever the two instruments correlate at, which is a number this page will not choose for you.
Against the one instrument’s 1.04

The top row is the best case and it is not four. Doubling the positions at a cross-correlation of zero doubles the bets, and doubling is the ceiling because the within-instrument 0.9247 is still there underneath, unchanged, on two of the six pairs. Then read down, and find the row your own two series put you in, because that is the only one that applies to you. At 0.6 the four positions carry 1.28 bets. You bought two more positions, two more spreads and two more lots of impact, and you bought a quarter of a bet.

The last row is the one to keep. At a cross-correlation equal to the within-instrument one, four positions on two instruments carry 1.06 bets, which is exactly the number lesson 74 measured for four rules on one instrument. The divisor cannot tell a second instrument from a fourth rule. Only the correlation goes in.

The two middle columns move in opposite directions down the same column of correlations, and that is the whole of the page. Every argument module 9 made was an argument for a smaller correlation, because a long-only book is worse the more alike its positions are. A spread is better the more alike they are, and at the 0.9247 lesson 74 measured on this course’s own rules the spread’s standard deviation is a fifth of the long-only pair’s.

Take the book lesson 81 graded and give it the second instrument it was missing, at the same 0.9247 the rules already carry, because that is the number this course has actually measured rather than assumed.
Four positions, all long: 1.06 independent bets, against 1.04 for two positions on one instrument.
The second instrument therefore bought 0.02 of a bet, for two more positions.
Two positions, one of them short: a standard deviation of 0.1940 against 0.9810, which is 5.06 times smaller.

Read those four lines against each other and the ranking is not close. Adding an instrument and keeping every leg long is the expensive repair and it buys two hundredths of a bet. Turning one leg over is the cheap one and it divides the day by five. Module 9 spent five lessons trying to find rules that were less alike, and the arithmetic says the profitable use of rules that are alike was available the whole time and needed one permission the course never granted.

Now price the permission, because it is not free and this course has already measured most of the bill. Two legs is two of lesson 12’s spreads on the way in and two on the way out, and two of lesson 59’s impact rather than one. The gross position is twice the net, so lesson 73’s warning applies exactly: every cost that scales with what you trade doubles while the standard deviation falls by 5.06. And the short leg carries a bill this course has never priced at all, which is what it costs to borrow the thing you are selling.

That a smaller standard deviation is a smaller risk. It is a smaller standard deviation on twice the gross position. Lesson 73 showed that the gross figure is where the costs live, and the second table changes the numerator of that ratio without touching the denominator. A spread at 0.9247 with a fifth of the daily movement and twice the bill is a better trade only if the edge survives the doubling, and nothing on this page establishes that it does.

That a correlation of 0.9247 stays 0.9247. Lesson 74 measured the median pair of this course’s own rules moving 0.0968 between two halves of one record, against 0.0205 under a null that says nothing changed, which is 4.71 times as much movement as chance produces. Price a spread at 0.9247 and live in a stretch where it is 0.5673, and its standard deviation rises from 0.1940 to 0.4651, which is 2.40 times. The trade that looked five times quieter is then two and a half times as loud as you sized it for, and it happens without any rule changing.

That this course measured a pair. It did not. There are sixty closes of one instrument in this course, and the cross-correlation is a parameter on every row of both tables. What is measured here is the divisor and the variance of a difference, which are arithmetic and hold for any two series, and what is borrowed is lesson 74’s 0.9247, which is a within-instrument number standing in for a between-instrument one. A reader who wants the finding on their own pair has to supply the pair.

Take daily closes for two things you would plausibly trade together, compute the correlation of their daily moves, and read the bet count off the first table. Ten minutes, and you end holding one number, the independent bets four positions across those two instruments would carry, which you compare against the 1.04 you carry now.

On the same two series, compute the standard deviation of holding both long and of holding one short, in whatever units your prices are in, and take the ratio. Half an hour, and you end holding one number, the factor by which turning one leg over shrinks your day, which you compare against the 5.06 on this page.

Split those two series down the middle, redo problem two on each half separately, and take the ratio of the two spread standard deviations. An evening, and you end holding one number, the factor by which your spread is louder in the worse half, which you compare against the 2.40 this page prints and which is the number you size against.
The 0.9247 this page spends, and the 0.0968 it moves by.
The 1.04 independent bets a second instrument is meant to repair.
